flawed_step: The uniqueness conclusion cannot be justified: strict, complete preferences guarantee existence of a stable matching, but not uniqueness.
counterexample: Let n=2. Men's preferences: m1: w1 > w2; m2: w2 > w1. Women's preferences: w1: m2 > m1; w2: m1 > m2. Matching A={(m1,w1),(m2,w2)} is stable: neither m1 nor m2 prefers the only unmatched woman to his partner. Matching B={(m1,w2),(m2,w1)} is also stable: for unmatched pair (m1,w1), w1 prefers her partner m2; for unmatched pair (m2,w2), w2 prefers her partner m1. Thus there are two distinct stable matchings despite all preferences being strict and complete.
assessment_summary: A direct proof attempt stops at the uniqueness claim. The explicit two-man, two-woman instance satisfies every hypothesis and has two carefully checked stable matchings, so the statement is false.
